questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.1 Aeronautical Decision-Making (ADM) models — 3P model
questions.keyword: 3P model Perceive Process Perform ADM sUAS
questions.text: A remote pilot is introduced to the FAA's Perceive-Process-Perform (3P) model of aeronautical decision-making during ground school. A complex sUAS mapping mission is being planned near a hospital with active helicopter traffic. Applying the 3P model, what does the 'Perceive' step require the pilot to do?

answers.text: Select the best risk management option and execute the flight plan without further delay
Perform an immediate risk mitigation action such as cancelling the flight before gathering any situational data
Identify and list all hazards present in the environment, including airspace conflicts, weather, equipment status, and personnel factors
Notify the FAA of all potential hazards identified before each commercial sUAS operation

explanations.a: Selecting and executing an option is the 'Perform' step; perception must precede processing and performing.
explanations.b: Perceive is the information-gathering step; taking action before perceiving hazards skips the foundational step of situational awareness.
explanations.c: The 'Perceive' step of the 3P model requires the pilot to actively scan the environment and identify all relevant hazards including weather, airspace, equipment, human factors, and external pressures; this situational awareness forms the basis for subsequent processing and action.
explanations.d: FAA notification is not part of the 3P model process; the model is an internal cognitive framework for individual aeronautical decision-making.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.1 ADM models — PAVE checklist
questions.keyword: PAVE checklist Pilot Aircraft enVironment External pressures
questions.text: A remote pilot uses the PAVE checklist as a preflight risk assessment tool. The pilot is under pressure from a client to fly in marginal weather to meet a project deadline. Which PAVE element specifically addresses this type of external pressure?

answers.text: The 'P' element — Pilot — because external pressure directly affects the pilot's personal minimums and go/no-go judgment
The 'A' element — Aircraft — because client-imposed schedules affect maintenance intervals and aircraft readiness
The 'E' element — External Pressures — which is specifically designed to identify non-safety pressures such as schedules, economic concerns, and client expectations
The 'V' element — enVironment — because weather-driven client pressure is an environmental rather than a personal factor

explanations.a: While external pressure affects the pilot's judgment (the P element), the PAVE checklist has a dedicated 'E' element specifically for external pressures; the Pilot element focuses on the pilot's own physical and mental state.
explanations.b: The Aircraft element addresses airworthiness and equipment status; client scheduling pressures are captured under external pressures, not aircraft condition.
explanations.c: The 'E' in PAVE stands for External Pressures — factors outside the cockpit (or control station) that push the pilot toward accepting risk, such as schedule demands, economic pressure, client expectations, and 'get-there-itis'; recognizing these pressures explicitly helps the pilot make an objective go/no-go decision.
explanations.d: The enVironment element in PAVE covers physical environmental factors like weather, airspace, and terrain; external pressures from clients and schedules have their own dedicated 'E' element in the checklist.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.2 Hazardous attitudes and antidotes
questions.keyword: hazardous attitude anti-authority 'don't tell me' antidote
questions.text: A remote pilot says, 'I've been flying drones commercially for three years and I know what I'm doing — I don't need to follow every FAA rule.' This attitude most closely matches which hazardous attitude, and what is its antidote?

answers.text: Anti-authority; the antidote is 'Follow the rules — they are usually right'
Invulnerability; the antidote is 'It could happen to me'
Impulsivity; the antidote is 'Not so fast — think first'
Macho; the antidote is 'Taking chances is foolish'

explanations.a: Anti-authority is the hazardous attitude of resenting or disregarding anyone who sets rules or limitations; the antidote is recognizing that 'rules are usually right' and exist because of hard-learned lessons; the pilot's dismissal of FAA regulations based on personal experience is a classic anti-authority statement.
explanations.b: Invulnerability involves believing that accidents happen to others, not to oneself; the expressed attitude here is about disrespecting rules, not about personal immunity from harm.
explanations.c: Impulsivity is characterized by feeling the need to do something, anything, immediately; disregarding regulatory authority is anti-authority, not impulsivity.
explanations.d: Macho involves proving one's toughness by taking risks; the expressed attitude about rules is anti-authority, not a risk-proving behavior.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.2 Hazardous attitudes and antidotes
questions.keyword: hazardous attitude invulnerability 'it won't happen to me'
questions.text: During a preflight brief, a remote pilot dismisses concerns about a possible loss of GPS signal near high-voltage power lines, saying 'I've flown near power lines dozens of times and never had an issue.' This statement reflects which hazardous attitude?

answers.text: Invulnerability — the pilot believes that because accidents haven't happened before, they won't happen in the future
Resignation — the pilot has given up trying to mitigate risks and accepts bad outcomes as inevitable
Anti-authority — the pilot is refusing to acknowledge the technical authority of those who identified the GPS interference risk
Impulsivity — the pilot is making a rushed decision to fly without properly thinking through the identified hazard

explanations.a: Invulnerability is the hazardous attitude that 'accidents happen to other people, not me'; past success without incident is a classic invulnerability trigger — the pilot is using a history of safe flights as evidence of immunity from future risk, which is statistically unsound.
explanations.b: Resignation involves a sense of helplessness; the pilot here is not resigned but is actively dismissing a known risk based on past success.
explanations.c: Anti-authority involves dismissing rules and authority figures; the pilot is not rejecting authority but rather dismissing a specific technical hazard based on personal experience.
explanations.d: Impulsivity requires rushing to action; the pilot is not rushing but rather rationalizing complacency about a known hazard, which is invulnerability.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.2 Hazardous attitudes and antidotes
questions.keyword: hazardous attitude macho risk-taking prove skill antidote
questions.text: A remote pilot deliberately flies the sUAS through a narrow gap between two buildings at high speed to impress a film crew, saying 'Anyone can fly slow and safe — real skill means pushing limits.' Which hazardous attitude does this demonstrate and what is its antidote?

answers.text: Macho — this pilot equates reckless high-speed gap flights with genuine skill; the antidote is recognizing that taking unnecessary chances is foolish, not impressive
Macho — the pilot is proving toughness by deliberately choosing a dangerous gap flight to impress the film crew; taking unnecessary risks to demonstrate ability is the hallmark of this attitude
Resignation — the pilot has accepted that spectacular maneuvers will eventually cause an accident and continues anyway
Anti-authority — the pilot is refusing to accept safe operating boundaries established by the manufacturer and FAA

explanations.a: Macho is the hazardous attitude of proving courage or superiority by taking needless risks; deliberately flying a narrow gap at high speed to impress a film crew exemplifies macho behavior; the antidote is the insight that taking unnecessary chances is foolish and that real professionalism is demonstrated by sound, safe decision-making.
explanations.b: Macho is the hazardous attitude of proving one's toughness, skill, or courage by taking unnecessary risks; deliberately flying through a narrow gap at high speed to impress observers is textbook macho behavior; the antidote is recognizing that taking chances is foolish — sound judgment and safety demonstrate greater professionalism than risky stunts.
explanations.c: Resignation involves accepting bad outcomes as inevitable and feeling helpless; the pilot here is actively seeking to create risk to demonstrate ability, which is macho behavior.
explanations.d: Anti-authority involves resisting rules and authority figures; the pilot is not resisting authority but deliberately choosing a dangerous maneuver to prove skill, which is the macho attitude.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.2 Hazardous attitudes and antidotes
questions.keyword: hazardous attitude resignation helpless fate antidote
questions.text: A remote pilot who is experiencing repeated equipment issues during a complex mission says, 'These things always go wrong for me — there's nothing I can do about it.' This statement reflects which hazardous attitude?

answers.text: Macho — the pilot is using fatalistic language to mask frustration with the technical difficulty
Anti-authority — the pilot is blaming the equipment manufacturer's authority for the failures
Impulsivity — the pilot feels urgency to finish the mission despite recognizing that problems exist
Resignation — the pilot feels that outcomes are beyond their control and that their actions make no difference

explanations.a: Macho involves risk-taking to prove ability; the passive, helpless attitude expressed here is resignation, not macho behavior.
explanations.b: Anti-authority involves resisting rules and authority; expressing helplessness about equipment is resignation, not anti-authority.
explanations.c: Impulsivity involves acting hastily; the pilot is not rushing to action but rather giving up, which is resignation.
explanations.d: Resignation is the hazardous attitude of feeling that nothing one does matters and that fate or bad luck controls outcomes; the antidote is 'I'm not helpless — I can make a difference'; pilots who feel resigned may fail to take corrective action when it could prevent an accident.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.3 Risk management — identifying and mitigating risk
questions.keyword: risk management 5 Ps Plan Plane Pilot Passengers Programming
questions.text: A remote pilot uses the 5 Ps checklist (Plan, Plane, Pilot, Passengers, Programming) as an in-flight risk management tool. Thirty minutes into a complex automated survey mission, the pilot realizes the battery level will not support the full planned flight time. Which 'P' element is being evaluated in this real-time assessment?

answers.text: Pilot — the pilot's personal minimums and decision-making capacity are being re-evaluated mid-flight
Passengers — the safety of any persons on the ground below is being reassessed based on flight time remaining
Programming — the autopilot's mission program is being assessed to determine whether it can be modified to reduce power consumption
Plan — the mission plan is being re-evaluated in light of new information about battery state, requiring a plan adjustment

explanations.a: The Pilot element covers the pilot's fitness, currency, and personal minimums; the battery evaluation is a mission planning factor, not a pilot-fitness assessment.
explanations.b: The Passengers element in the original 5 Ps framework covers passengers or persons on board, not ground-level third parties; battery status is a plan issue.
explanations.c: While reprogramming the autopilot might be a mitigation action, the assessment of whether the current plan is viable based on battery state is a Plan evaluation.
explanations.d: The Plan element covers whether the intended mission can be completed as designed; discovering that battery capacity is insufficient to execute the full plan requires re-evaluating and modifying the plan, which is the Plan 'P' in the 5 Ps framework.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.3 Risk management — identifying and mitigating risk
questions.keyword: risk management IMSAFE checklist personal readiness pilot
questions.text: A remote pilot reviews the IMSAFE personal readiness checklist before a complex commercial sUAS operation. What does the 'M' in IMSAFE stand for, and what condition does it evaluate?

answers.text: 'M' stands for Medication; it evaluates whether the pilot is taking any prescription or over-the-counter drugs that could impair judgment or motor skills
'M' stands for Mission; it evaluates whether the planned mission is within the pilot's training and experience level
'M' stands for Meteorology; it evaluates whether current and forecast weather conditions are within the pilot's personal minimums
'M' stands for Motivation; it evaluates whether the pilot has a positive attitude and sufficient desire to complete the planned mission

explanations.a: The IMSAFE checklist covers: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, and Emotion/Eating; 'M' stands for Medication and requires the pilot to evaluate whether any drugs — prescription or over-the-counter — could impair aviation-critical performance such as reaction time, judgment, or coordination.
explanations.b: The Mission element is not part of the IMSAFE acronym; the checklist focuses on personal pilot readiness, not mission appropriateness.
explanations.c: Meteorology is not an IMSAFE element; weather assessment is covered by other preflight tools; IMSAFE focuses exclusively on the pilot's personal physical and mental state.
explanations.d: Motivation is not an IMSAFE element; while attitude is relevant to pilot performance, the IMSAFE checklist's 'M' specifically addresses medication effects.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.4 Emergency procedures — loss of control link
questions.keyword: loss of link failsafe RTH behavior preflight setting
questions.text: A remote pilot's sUAS experiences a complete loss of control link signal at 350 ft AGL during a mapping mission over agricultural land. No persons are in the flight area. The sUAS is equipped with a return-to-home (RTH) failsafe set to activate upon link loss. Under 14 CFR Part 107 and safety principles, what is the most important preflight action that determines the safety of this RTH sequence?

answers.text: Verifying that the RTH altitude is set high enough to clear all obstacles between the current position and the home point before the mission begins
Calibrating the compass immediately before each flight so the aircraft always knows the direction of north during RTH
Setting the RTH speed to the maximum allowable to minimize the time the aircraft spends flying without positive control
Enabling the aircraft's strobe light to activate automatically during RTH so visual observers can track the returning sUAS

explanations.a: If the RTH altitude is set too low, the returning aircraft may collide with a building, tree, tower, or terrain feature between its current position and the home point; verifying that the RTH altitude clears all known obstacles along the return path is the most critical RTH-specific preflight check.
explanations.b: Compass calibration is important but is not the most critical RTH-specific safety check; the RTH altitude relative to terrain and obstacles is the primary safety concern during automated return.
explanations.c: Maximum RTH speed reduces obstacle avoidance reaction time and increases airspace conflict potential; RTH altitude adequacy is a more fundamental safety concern than return speed.
explanations.d: Strobe activation during RTH is helpful but secondary to ensuring the aircraft can physically clear all obstacles during the automated return; obstacle clearance altitude is the primary concern.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.4 Emergency procedures — loss of control link
questions.keyword: loss of control link manual intervention attempt first
questions.text: During a commercial sUAS inspection, the control link drops and the aircraft begins an unintended slow drift toward a highway. The pilot attempts to regain link by moving closer to the aircraft. After 15 seconds the link is restored. Under ADM principles, which immediate action should the pilot have taken when the link was first lost?

answers.text: Attempt to regain the link while simultaneously alerting the visual observer to track the aircraft and evaluate its trajectory relative to hazards
Immediately activate the failsafe RTH and do nothing further until the aircraft returns to the home point
Contact the nearest ATC facility by radio to declare an emergency and request priority handling for the uncontrolled sUAS
Leave the area immediately to comply with the emergency deviation provision of 107.21 before attempting any recovery

explanations.a: The appropriate immediate response to link loss combines active recovery attempts (moving to improve link quality, checking for interference) with ongoing visual tracking through the visual observer; simultaneously evaluating the aircraft's drift toward hazards allows informed decisions about whether to let RTH proceed or intervene otherwise.
explanations.b: Relying solely on RTH without attempting link recovery or monitoring the aircraft's trajectory may result in RTH completing on a collision course if the failsafe altitude or behavior is not configured correctly.
explanations.c: ATC contact is not the immediate first response to a link loss; most sUAS link losses resolve within seconds; if the aircraft becomes a safety hazard to manned aviation, that is a separate consideration.
explanations.d: The emergency deviation provision allows deviation from rules to meet an emergency; abandoning the area during a link loss does not address the immediate hazard of an uncontrolled aircraft drifting toward a highway.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.5 Emergency procedures — fly-away and uncontrolled flight
questions.keyword: flyaway prevention pre-flight checks geofencing limitation
questions.text: A remote pilot experiences a flyaway event where the sUAS departs the operating area at high speed despite maximum control inputs. After the event, the manufacturer confirms a compass calibration error caused the flight controller to misidentify north and command full speed in the wrong direction. Which preflight action would have been most likely to prevent this event?

answers.text: Performing a full compass calibration at the launch site on the day of the flight, especially if the aircraft has been transported to a new location with different magnetic environment
Increasing the maximum control input sensitivity so the pilot's corrective inputs would have been fast enough to overcome the flight controller error
Using a backup mechanical compass mounted on the aircraft that provides independent heading reference independent of the electronic flight controller
Setting the maximum speed limit to 10 knots to prevent the sUAS from flying away faster than the pilot can walk to recover it

explanations.a: Compass calibration errors are a known cause of flyaway events; performing a fresh calibration at the operating site, particularly after transport (which can expose the aircraft to different magnetic environments), is the most effective preventive measure against compass-induced flyaways.
explanations.b: Increasing control sensitivity does not address the root cause of the compass error; if the flight controller is misidentifying north, increased stick inputs will still send the aircraft in the wrong direction.
explanations.c: A mechanical backup compass provides heading reference to the pilot but does not feed into the flight controller; the flight controller's compass error would persist regardless of what a mechanical compass reads.
explanations.d: A 10-knot speed limit would reduce the severity of a flyaway but would not prevent one; the root cause is the compass calibration error, not the maximum speed setting.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.5 Emergency procedures — fly-away and uncontrolled flight
questions.keyword: flyaway over populated area emergency landing safest available
questions.text: A remote pilot has experienced an sUAS flyaway and the aircraft is heading toward a populated suburban neighborhood. The pilot has regained partial manual control but cannot stop forward flight. The aircraft will impact the ground in approximately 25 seconds. Which decision best reflects sound aeronautical decision-making under this emergency?

answers.text: Direct the aircraft toward the least-populated or completely open area within reach, accepting a controlled crash over an open field rather than an uncontrolled impact near people
Command maximum altitude to gain time and wait for the flight controller to self-correct the fault before the aircraft runs out of battery
Immediately land in the nearest yard regardless of whether people are visible, because any ground contact minimizes the risk of aerial collision
Continue attempting full control inputs while calling 911 to alert authorities; do not deviate from the original flight path

explanations.a: When facing an imminent uncontrolled impact, the best ADM outcome is to direct the aircraft toward the area that minimizes risk to people; guiding the aircraft to a controlled crash in an open field — even at cost to the aircraft — is consistent with the principle of minimizing harm to third parties.
explanations.b: Commanding maximum altitude increases flight time but does not resolve the control fault; delaying impact near populated areas increases rather than decreases risk.
explanations.c: Landing in the nearest yard regardless of occupancy risks injury to people in that space; the goal is to find the area with fewest people at risk, not simply the nearest ground contact point.
explanations.d: Continuing unchanged flight inputs while calling 911 does not address the immediate hazard; emergency deviation under 107.21 permits and requires the pilot to take necessary action to minimize risk to people.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.6 Emergency procedures — motor failure and partial loss of thrust
questions.keyword: motor failure multirotor yaw spin attitude control loss
questions.text: A remote pilot's hexacopter loses one motor mid-flight, causing the aircraft to begin an uncontrolled yaw spin. The aircraft is at 200 ft AGL over an open field. Under ADM principles, what is the most important immediate action?

answers.text: Increase throttle to maximum to gain altitude and give the flight controller time to compensate for the motor loss with the remaining five motors
Cut all throttle immediately so the aircraft auto-rotates to the ground like a helicopter in engine failure
Activate the return-to-home sequence immediately so the aircraft uses GPS to navigate back to the launch point despite the motor failure
Attempt to reduce the yaw spin using rudder commands while simultaneously descending and landing as quickly as possible in the open field below

explanations.a: Increasing throttle to maximum during an uncontrolled yaw spin amplifies rotor torque imbalance and can worsen the spin; gaining altitude also increases potential harm if control is further degraded.
explanations.b: Multi-rotor aircraft cannot autorotate; cutting throttle causes uncontrolled free fall, which is worse than a partially controlled descent.
explanations.c: RTH requires navigational control; in an active yaw spin the aircraft may not be able to execute a coherent RTH sequence; the pilot should attempt immediate manual descent rather than depend on automation during a mechanical failure.
explanations.d: After a motor failure causing yaw instability, the priority is to control the descent rate and guide the aircraft to the open field below as quickly as safely possible; some yaw control inputs may partially stabilize rotation while a rapid but controlled descent minimizes altitude and potential energy before an inevitable forced landing.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.7 Situational awareness — loss and recovery
questions.keyword: situational awareness spatial disorientation orientation recovery visual reference
questions.text: A remote pilot loses visual orientation of the sUAS and is unsure which direction the aircraft is facing. The aircraft's position lights (red left, green right) are not visible from the pilot's current position. Under ADM principles, what is the best immediate action to recover situational awareness?

answers.text: Apply full forward stick and observe which direction the aircraft moves; movement toward the pilot indicates the nose is pointed at the pilot
Activate the home-lock mode and release all sticks to prevent inadvertent inputs while re-establishing situational awareness
Immediately command the aircraft to climb to maximum altitude so it becomes a visible speck and the orientation can be determined from any angle
Hover the aircraft in place without any control inputs; contact the visual observer for a position and orientation assessment before taking any further action

explanations.a: Applying full forward stick to a disoriented aircraft risks a rapid departure in an unknown direction; control inputs without orientation knowledge can worsen the situation.
explanations.b: Home-lock mode behavior varies by manufacturer and may not be available; the correct first step is to eliminate control inputs and consult the visual observer for orientation recovery.
explanations.c: Climbing to maximum altitude increases airspace risk and creates a difficult-to-control high-altitude situation; it does not reliably solve the orientation problem.
explanations.d: Stopping all control inputs and hovering in place while the visual observer — who has a clear view of the aircraft — provides orientation information is the safest approach to recovering situational awareness; the visual observer's external perspective is specifically designed for this scenario.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.7 Situational awareness — loss and recovery
questions.keyword: get-there-itis mission completion pressure ADM continuation bias
questions.text: A remote pilot has been hired to complete a critical infrastructure inspection under a tight client deadline. Weather has deteriorated to visibility of 3 miles and a 600-ft ceiling, exactly at Part 107 minimums. The pilot feels strong pressure to complete the job today. Which cognitive trap is the pilot most at risk of falling into, and what is the correct ADM response?

answers.text: Scud running — the pilot is tempted to fly below cloud bases to maintain visual reference; the ADM response is to climb above the clouds to safer altitudes

Startle response — the pilot will experience a physiological startle reaction to the deteriorating conditions; the ADM response is to activate the autopilot and allow the sUAS to manage the approach autonomously
Spatial disorientation — deteriorating weather may cause the pilot to lose orientation; the ADM response is to switch to instrument-only flight using the sUAS's onboard flight controller

Get-there-itis (plan continuation bias) — the pilot is tempted to push forward despite conditions at the regulatory edge; the ADM response is to establish personal minimums above the regulatory floor and be willing to postpone or cancel the mission

explanations.a: Scud running involves flying at very low altitudes under deteriorating cloud bases in manned aircraft; while the concept is related, the cognitive trap here is specifically plan continuation bias driven by deadline pressure.
explanations.b: Startle response is a physiological reaction to sudden unexpected events; the pilot is not experiencing a startle event but rather a planned continuation under pressure; autopilot activation does not address the decision-making challenge.
explanations.c: Spatial disorientation is a different hazard; the pilot's challenge here is decision-making under external pressure, not orientation loss; sUAS also do not have instrument-only flight capability analogous to manned IFR.
explanations.d: Get-there-itis (also called plan continuation bias) is the tendency to continue a planned course of action even as conditions deteriorate; flying at the exact regulatory minimum with strong deadline pressure is a hallmark scenario; sound ADM requires personal minimums to include a buffer above regulatory floors, and the willingness to postpone despite client pressure.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.8 CRM — crew coordination and task management
questions.keyword: CRM crew resource management crew briefing task allocation
questions.text: Before a complex sUAS operation at a crowded outdoor event, a remote pilot holds a crew briefing assigning specific roles to the visual observer, a safety spotter, and a ground safety coordinator. This briefing represents which Crew Resource Management (CRM) principle?

answers.text: Assertiveness — the remote pilot is asserting authority over the crew to establish a chain of command for the operation
Sterile cockpit enforcement — the briefing establishes which crew members may speak during which phases of flight
Complacency avoidance — the briefing is designed to prevent the crew from becoming too comfortable with repeated sUAS operations
Task management and workload distribution — allocating specific roles reduces the remote PIC's workload and ensures all critical functions are covered by appropriate crew members

explanations.a: While a briefing does establish authority, the specific CRM principle demonstrated by role assignment and task delegation is workload management, not assertiveness as a standalone concept.
explanations.b: Sterile cockpit is the concept of limiting non-essential communication during critical phases; the briefing here is defining roles and communication protocols, which is workload management.
explanations.c: Complacency avoidance is a CRM concern addressed through challenge-and-response checklists and standardized procedures; a pre-flight role briefing is primarily a workload management tool.
explanations.d: CRM principles emphasize effective task management and workload distribution; assigning specific roles to crew members ensures that critical functions (VLOS, crowd monitoring, safety coordination) are handled by dedicated personnel rather than overwhelming a single operator, which is a core CRM objective.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.8 CRM — crew coordination and task management
questions.keyword: CRM assertiveness speaking up unsafe conditions corrective action
questions.text: During an sUAS operation, a visual observer notices the remote pilot has not heard a radio call from an approaching helicopter. The visual observer is hesitant to interrupt the remote pilot who is focused on a complex maneuver. Under CRM principles, what should the visual observer do?

answers.text: Wait for the current maneuver to complete before mentioning the helicopter to avoid distracting the pilot during a critical moment
Write a note and pass it to the remote pilot to minimize verbal interruption during the maneuver
Immediately and clearly alert the remote pilot to the approaching helicopter regardless of the current maneuver, using a pre-briefed alert call if available
Attempt to contact the helicopter pilot on CTAF independently and ask them to deviate around the sUAS operating area

explanations.a: Waiting to report an approaching helicopter until after a maneuver is complete could allow a collision to develop; time-critical safety information must be communicated immediately regardless of the current maneuver.
explanations.b: Written notes are not an appropriate communication method for urgent safety-of-flight information; verbal or pre-briefed alert calls are required for time-critical hazards.
explanations.c: CRM principles, particularly assertiveness, require crew members to speak up immediately when safety is at risk; the visual observer's primary function is to enhance the remote pilot's situational awareness, and alerting the pilot to an approaching helicopter is exactly this function — it should be done immediately using clear, direct communication.
explanations.d: The visual observer's role is to support the remote pilot's situational awareness, not to take independent radio action; the pilot must be informed immediately so they can yield right of way and take appropriate evasive action.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.9 Emergency procedures — battery fire and thermal runaway
questions.keyword: LiPo thermal runaway fire landing immediate containment
questions.text: During flight, a remote pilot notices smoke and smell of burning coming from the sUAS during a building inspection at 150 ft AGL. The flight controller still shows nominal battery voltage. What is the correct immediate action?

answers.text: Continue the inspection because the battery voltage reading is nominal, indicating the odor is likely from the motor windings and not a battery fire
Increase altitude immediately to 400 ft AGL to get the aircraft away from the building and any ground-level personnel before the fault is further evaluated
Land the aircraft immediately in the safest available open area and move it away from people and flammable materials once on the ground; treat it as a potential thermal runaway event
Command the aircraft to return-to-home to retrieve it at the launch point where fire suppression equipment is staged

explanations.a: Nominal voltage does not rule out a battery fire; thermal runaway can produce smoke and gas before voltage collapses; continuing the flight in this condition risks in-flight disintegration and fire debris raining over the building and personnel.
explanations.b: Climbing with a potentially burning aircraft increases risk; the overriding priority is to get the aircraft on the ground as quickly as possible in the safest available area.
explanations.c: Smoke and burning smell from an sUAS in flight indicate potential LiPo thermal runaway or motor/ESC fire; the correct immediate action is to land immediately in the safest available open area, clear of people and flammable materials; once on the ground, do not pick up a burning LiPo with bare hands and keep personnel back.
explanations.d: RTH takes time and directs a potentially burning aircraft to the launch point where crew members are present; immediate landing in the nearest safe open area is the priority over navigating back to the home point.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.3 Risk management — identifying and mitigating risk
questions.keyword: risk severity probability matrix go no-go decision tool
questions.text: A remote pilot uses a risk severity matrix before each flight to evaluate identified hazards. For the risk associated with a 20-knot crosswind forecast for the planned sUAS corridor inspection, the pilot rates severity as 'moderate' and probability as 'likely.' Based on standard risk matrix principles, what should this combination indicate?

answers.text: The flight should proceed without restrictions because 'moderate' severity means the risk is manageable and 'likely' probability means the pilot should expect the risk and prepare normally
The probability rating should be the sole decision factor; since the event is 'likely,' the severity is irrelevant and the pilot should cancel immediately
The risk matrix is only applicable to aviation weather hazards; personnel and equipment risks are evaluated using different tools under the FAA's safety management system

The combination indicates an elevated or high risk level that requires the pilot to implement active mitigations such as reducing the operational area, waiting for improved conditions, or cancelling the flight

explanations.a: 'Moderate' severity combined with 'likely' probability typically produces an elevated or high risk rating in a standard risk matrix; this combination does not automatically authorize proceeding without mitigation.
explanations.b: Both severity and probability must be considered together to derive a meaningful risk rating; using only probability while ignoring severity produces an incomplete and misleading risk assessment.
explanations.c: Risk matrices are applicable to all hazard categories in aviation safety management, not only weather; personnel factors, equipment issues, and operational environment are all evaluated using risk assessment tools.
explanations.d: In a standard risk matrix, the combination of moderate severity and high/likely probability typically produces an elevated or high overall risk rating; this level generally requires active risk mitigation strategies such as restricting the mission scope, waiting for better conditions, or cancelling if mitigations are insufficient to bring risk to an acceptable level.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.4 Emergency procedures — loss of control link
questions.keyword: lost link procedure pilot action regulatory obligation deviation
questions.text: A remote pilot's sUAS loses control link and the RTH failsafe activates, bringing the aircraft to a landing point different from the intended recovery zone. During the RTH descent, the aircraft briefly enters Class D airspace that was not authorized for this operation. No manned aircraft were in the vicinity. After the aircraft lands safely, what are the pilot's regulatory obligations?

answers.text: No obligation exists because the airspace entry was caused by an automated failsafe, not a deliberate pilot action, making the pilot legally exempt from reporting requirements
The pilot must file a NOTAM within 24 hours describing the unauthorized airspace entry and its cause
The pilot deviated from Part 107 rules due to an in-flight emergency; upon FAA request, the pilot must submit a written report explaining the deviation under 14 CFR 107.21
The pilot must notify the nearest FSDO by telephone within 2 hours of the unauthorized Class D airspace entry

explanations.a: Automated failsafe behavior does not remove regulatory responsibility from the remote PIC; the PIC is responsible for the aircraft's conduct at all times, including during automated operations.
explanations.b: Filing a NOTAM is not the reporting mechanism for in-flight emergency deviations; NOTAMs notify airspace users of hazards, not regulatory deviations.
explanations.c: Under 14 CFR 107.21, a remote PIC may deviate from any Part 107 rule to the extent necessary during an in-flight emergency; after the emergency, the PIC must submit a written report explaining the deviation if the FAA requests one; this is the applicable reporting obligation for an emergency-induced airspace entry.
explanations.d: A 2-hour FSDO telephone notification is not specified in Part 107 for this type of event; the obligation under 107.21 is a written report upon FAA request, not a proactive telephone notification.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.1 ADM models — DECIDE model
questions.keyword: DECIDE model Detect Estimate Choose Identify Do Evaluate
questions.text: A remote pilot applies the DECIDE model during a mission when the sUAS suddenly experiences a significant GPS signal loss. Working through the DECIDE steps, the pilot first detects the GPS loss. What does the 'E' step — Estimate — require in this situation?

answers.text: Execute an immediate RTH command before any further assessment, because action must always precede evaluation in an emergency
Eliminate the hazard by activating the backup navigation mode before estimating the scope of the problem
Evaluate the outcome of the corrective action taken and determine whether the problem has been resolved
Estimate the need for action by evaluating how the GPS loss affects current navigation, stabilization, and planned mission execution, including potential risks if the condition is not addressed

explanations.a: Executing RTH immediately is an action step; the DECIDE model requires estimation of the problem's scope and impact before choosing an action.
explanations.b: Eliminating or activating backup systems is an action step ('Do') that follows choosing a course of action; estimation must precede the action choice.
explanations.c: Evaluating the outcome of a corrective action is the final 'E' (Evaluate) step in the DECIDE model, not the second 'E' (Estimate); these are two distinct steps.
explanations.d: The 'E' step in the DECIDE model (Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate) requires the pilot to estimate the significance of the detected problem — in this case, how GPS loss affects flight stability, navigation accuracy, obstacle avoidance, and mission safety — before choosing a course of action.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.10 Human factors — fatigue effects on performance
questions.keyword: fatigue performance degradation vigilance attention sUAS operator
questions.text: A remote pilot has been conducting back-to-back commercial sUAS flights for 9 hours in hot summer conditions with minimal food and water. The pilot feels tired but wants to complete one final 20-minute mapping flight before packing up. Under 14 CFR 107.17 and ADM principles, what should the pilot consider?

answers.text: Proceed with the flight because 9 hours is well within the FAA's maximum 12-hour duty day for remote pilots under Part 107
Proceed if the final flight is a simple automated mission requiring minimal manual control inputs
Assess whether fatigue has reached a level where it would interfere with safe sUAS operation; if so, cancel the flight because fatigued operation violates 107.17
Delegate the final flight to the visual observer who has been monitoring but not actively operating throughout the day

explanations.a: Part 107 does not establish a maximum 12-hour duty day; the regulation at 107.17 requires the pilot not to fly if a physical or mental condition would interfere with safe operation, regardless of hours worked.
explanations.b: Fatigue affects judgment, vigilance, and response time even during automated missions where the pilot must monitor for anomalies and respond to emergencies; automated flight does not eliminate the need for an alert operator.
explanations.c: Under 14 CFR 107.17, the remote PIC must self-assess fitness before each flight; fatigue after a long hot duty day is a known performance impairment; if the pilot determines fatigue would interfere with safe operation, the flight must be cancelled — this is not merely advisory, it is a regulatory requirement.
explanations.d: The visual observer is not a certificated remote PIC and cannot legally assume command of the sUAS; remote PIC responsibilities cannot be transferred to the visual observer.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.10 Human factors — stress effects on performance
questions.keyword: stress acute chronic performance degradation tunnel vision
questions.text: During a high-stakes commercial sUAS inspection near energized power lines, a remote pilot experiences acute stress causing narrowed attention and tunnel vision focused only on the aircraft's proximity to the lines. The pilot fails to notice a news helicopter approaching from behind. Which human performance concept does this scenario illustrate?

answers.text: Channelized attention — acute stress can cause a pilot to focus so intensely on one aspect of the task that other critical information is not processed
Cognitive drift — the pilot's attention has drifted from the primary task of power line avoidance to the secondary task of helicopter detection
Target fixation — the pilot has become overly focused on landing the aircraft on the power line structure rather than avoiding it
Scud running — the pilot is mentally flying below the safety minimums to get closer to the inspection target

explanations.a: Channelized attention (also called target fixation in some contexts) describes the narrowing of attention under stress to a single aspect of the task at the expense of broader situational awareness; in this case, intense focus on the power line proximity causes the pilot to miss the approaching helicopter — a classic channelized attention failure.
explanations.b: Cognitive drift describes unintentional mental wandering away from the task at hand; the pilot is not drifting but is hyper-focused on one specific task, which is channelized attention.
explanations.c: Target fixation typically describes fixating on a collision target to the point of flying into it; the pilot here is avoiding the power lines, not fixating on impact with them.
explanations.d: Scud running is a manned aviation phenomenon involving low-altitude flight under deteriorating cloud bases; it is not applicable to the stress-induced attention narrowing described in this scenario.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.3 Risk management — personal minimums
questions.keyword: personal minimums conservative buffer above regulatory floor safety margin
questions.text: A remote pilot establishes personal minimums of 5 SM visibility and 800 ft AGL ceiling for commercial sUAS operations, even though Part 107 allows 3 SM visibility and no specific ceiling minimum (only cloud clearance rules apply). Why is establishing personal minimums above the regulatory floor considered sound ADM?

answers.text: Personal minimums above regulatory floors are required by FAA regulations; pilots who fly at the exact regulatory minimum violate the spirit of Part 107

Personal minimums above regulatory floors are only relevant for student pilots; experienced remote pilots should fly at the exact regulatory minimum to demonstrate full utilization of their certification
Personal minimums only need to exceed regulatory minimums for night operations; daytime operations can use the exact regulatory minimums without safety concern

Personal minimums provide a safety buffer that accounts for changing conditions, the tendency for weather to deteriorate, human performance variability, and the lack of immediate recovery options when conditions are at the regulatory edge

explanations.a: Personal minimums above regulatory floors are a best practice recommendation, not a regulatory requirement; the FAA strongly encourages them but does not mandate specific personal minimums above Part 107 regulatory floors.
explanations.b: Experience level does not change the value of personal minimums; in fact, experienced professionals in all aviation sectors use conservative personal minimums precisely because their experience has taught them the value of safety buffers.
explanations.c: Personal minimums benefit all operations regardless of time of day; the reasoning for conservative minimums applies equally to daytime flights.
explanations.d: Sound ADM recognizes that weather conditions can deteriorate during a flight, human performance is variable under fatigue or stress, and being at the exact regulatory edge leaves no margin for unexpected changes; personal minimums provide a buffer that allows the pilot to abort before reaching the regulatory limit.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.11 Emergency procedures — loss of GPS and GNSS outage
questions.keyword: GPS loss attitude mode position hold lost manual control challenge
questions.text: During a complex automated survey, a remote pilot's sUAS transitions from GPS-assisted flight to attitude mode after losing GPS signal due to radio frequency interference. The aircraft begins drifting in the wind. The pilot is accustomed to GPS-assisted flight and has limited experience with manual attitude mode. Which risk factor is highlighted by this scenario?

answers.text: Over-reliance on GPS automation leading to inadequate manual flying proficiency; the pilot lacks the practiced skill to manually control the aircraft when automation fails
The aircraft's attitude mode is malfunctioning; GPS loss should not cause attitude mode to behave differently from GPS mode for a properly calibrated sUAS
The risk of GPS interference at survey altitudes where magnetic field anomalies are strongest between 200 and 400 ft AGL
Insufficient battery capacity; GPS mode uses significantly more power than attitude mode, causing premature voltage drop in the interfered environment

explanations.a: Over-reliance on GPS-assisted automation is a significant sUAS pilot proficiency risk; when GPS fails, the aircraft reverts to a mode requiring more active manual control; pilots who have not maintained manual flying proficiency may be unable to manage the aircraft effectively in attitude mode, particularly in wind.
explanations.b: GPS loss causing reversion to attitude mode is expected behavior, not a malfunction; attitude mode's position-drift-without-correction behavior is the normal result of losing GPS-based position hold.
explanations.c: There is no well-established maximum GPS interference zone at 200–400 ft AGL due to magnetic field anomalies; RF interference from ground-based sources is the more typical GPS disruption cause and is not altitude-banded in this way.
explanations.d: GPS mode and attitude mode have relatively comparable power draw; battery capacity is not the primary risk factor illustrated by the pilot's control difficulty in attitude mode.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.1 ADM models — single-pilot resource management
questions.keyword: single pilot resource management automation management systems monitoring
questions.text: A remote pilot operating solo (without a visual observer) is flying an automated sUAS mission using a tablet-based ground control station. The pilot becomes so absorbed in the tablet display reviewing live sensor data that they stop visually scanning the aircraft and sky. Which single-pilot resource management (SRM) failure is occurring?

answers.text: Task prioritization failure — the pilot has deprioritized automation monitoring in favor of manual control inputs, creating a gap in the mission data stream
Cognitive reserve depletion — the pilot has used all available mental bandwidth on sensor review, leaving no capacity for automation monitoring
Workload over-management — the pilot is managing workload too conservatively by reducing manual inputs when automation handles the flight
Automation complacency — the pilot is over-trusting the automated system to manage the aircraft while neglecting the required visual scanning and situational awareness duties

explanations.a: The pilot is not prioritizing manual control inputs; the failure is excessive trust in automation at the expense of visual scanning — this is automation complacency.
explanations.b: Cognitive reserve depletion describes a real human performance concept, but the specific failure illustrated here — trusting automation while neglecting scan duties — is most precisely called automation complacency in the SRM framework.
explanations.c: Workload over-management would involve unnecessarily reducing tasks; the pilot is not managing workload conservatively but is simply failing to maintain essential visual scanning.
explanations.d: Automation complacency occurs when a pilot over-trusts automated systems and reduces active monitoring of the environment; in this case, absorption in the data display while neglecting visual scanning allows airspace conflicts, equipment anomalies, or emerging hazards to go undetected — a classic SRM failure in automated operations.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.9 Emergency procedures — battery fire and thermal runaway
questions.keyword: LiPo post-crash fire suppression sand dry chemical water
questions.text: An sUAS crashes and the LiPo battery begins venting gas and then ignites. A fire extinguisher is available at the scene. What fire suppression approach is most effective for a LiPo battery fire, and what should be avoided?

answers.text: Use a standard ABC dry chemical extinguisher at close range; avoid water as it reacts explosively with lithium compounds in the battery cells
Use large amounts of water or a Class D metal fire extinguisher; avoid ABC dry chemical agents as they are ineffective on lithium battery fires
Use sand to smother the fire and prevent oxygen access; large quantities of water can also cool the cells; avoid Class B foam which spreads burning electrolyte
Allow the battery to burn out completely without any suppression; attempting to extinguish a LiPo fire increases the risk of toxic gas inhalation

explanations.a: ABC dry chemical extinguishers have limited effectiveness on LiPo fires; lithium battery fires generate their own oxygen supply and can reignite; water is not explosively reactive with LiPo batteries the way it is with pure lithium metal.
explanations.b: While water can help cool a LiPo battery, it is not the primary recommended agent; large amounts of water applied correctly can suppress cell temperature, but Class D extinguishers are for combustible metal fires such as pure lithium, not lithium-ion polymer cells.
explanations.c: For LiPo battery fires, sand is effective at smothering the fire and preventing re-ignition; large quantities of water can help cool the cells and reduce thermal runaway propagation; Class B foam should be avoided as it may spread burning electrolyte; personnel should stay upwind of toxic fumes.
explanations.d: Allowing a LiPo fire to burn uncontrolled in proximity to people, vehicles, or flammable materials is not appropriate; controlled suppression with appropriate agents is the correct response.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.12 NASA ASRS voluntary reporting program
questions.keyword: NASA ASRS Aviation Safety Reporting System immunity protection
questions.text: A remote pilot inadvertently violates a TFR during a flight and wants to protect themselves while contributing to aviation safety data. The pilot decides to file a report with the NASA Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS). What protection does an ASRS report provide?

answers.text: An ASRS report provides complete immunity from any FAA civil penalty or certificate action for any violation, regardless of severity or intent

An ASRS report filed within 10 calendar days of the incident provides the pilot with protection from FAA certificate suspension, though civil penalties may still apply for criminal or intentional violations
An ASRS report guarantees a full waiver of all violations and automatically expunges any prior enforcement action from the pilot's record
An ASRS report has no legal protection; it is a voluntary safety data collection system with no regulatory impact on FAA enforcement actions

explanations.a: ASRS protection is not absolute immunity; it does not protect against criminal violations or intentional acts, and civil penalties can still apply in certain cases.
explanations.b: The FAA honors ASRS reports as part of its safety compliance philosophy; a timely ASRS report (filed within 10 calendar days of the incident) can shield a pilot from certificate suspension for inadvertent violations; however, the protection has limits and does not apply to criminal acts, intentional violations, or accidents.
explanations.c: ASRS does not guarantee expungement of prior enforcement records; it provides specific protections for reported incidents under defined conditions.
explanations.d: ASRS does have regulatory significance; the FAA's Aviation Safety Action Program and related policies give ASRS reports meaningful enforcement protection, making this statement incorrect.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.2 Hazardous attitudes and antidotes
questions.keyword: hazardous attitude impulsivity act immediately without thinking antidote
questions.text: During a high-energy sUAS aerial chase sequence for a film production, a warning appears on the ground control station indicating a potential GPS anomaly. Without reading the full warning message, the remote pilot immediately switches to manual mode and makes aggressive stick inputs. This behavior reflects which hazardous attitude?

answers.text: Macho — the pilot is demonstrating skill by switching modes quickly under pressure
Anti-authority — the pilot is refusing to follow the flight controller's automated guidance
Impulsivity — the pilot acted immediately without thinking through the warning or its implications
Invulnerability — the pilot believes aggressive manual inputs cannot cause harm

explanations.a: Macho involves deliberately taking risks to prove ability; responding to a warning without reading it is impulsivity — acting before thinking.
explanations.b: Anti-authority involves resisting rules and authority; the pilot is not rejecting authority but rather reacting without adequate information processing.
explanations.c: Impulsivity is the hazardous attitude of feeling compelled to do something, anything, immediately without thinking it through; not reading the full warning before making aggressive inputs is a textbook impulsive response; the antidote is 'Not so fast — think first.'
explanations.d: Invulnerability involves believing harm cannot happen to oneself; the pilot's hasty response to a warning is impulsivity, not a belief in personal immunity.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.3 Risk management — identifying and mitigating risk
questions.keyword: risk mitigation hierarchy elimination substitution administrative control
questions.text: An sUAS operator is developing a safety plan for operations over a construction site with workers below. The operator identifies the risk of sUAS impact on workers if a propeller failure occurs. Applying the hierarchy of risk controls, which mitigation is most preferred?

answers.text: Issue hard hats and safety vests to all construction workers below the sUAS flight path (administrative and PPE controls)
Post a spotter to watch the sUAS and shout a warning if the aircraft appears to be failing (administrative control)
Use a Category 2 or higher sUAS certified to meet injury severity limits, or fly at times when workers are not beneath the flight path (elimination or substitution of the hazard exposure)
Develop a written emergency response procedure for workers to follow if the sUAS crashes (administrative control)

explanations.a: PPE and administrative controls are at the lower end of the hierarchy of risk controls; they mitigate rather than eliminate the hazard and should be used when higher-level controls are not feasible.
explanations.b: A spotter warning is an administrative control; it does not reduce the probability of a propeller failure or eliminate the exposure of workers to the hazard.
explanations.c: The hierarchy of risk controls prioritizes elimination of the hazard first, then substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, and PPE last; flying when workers are not present eliminates the exposure, and using a certified injury-reducing sUAS represents an engineering/substitution control — both are higher in the hierarchy than administrative controls or PPE.
explanations.d: Emergency response procedures are administrative controls at the lower end of the hierarchy; they do not prevent the hazard from occurring.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.6 Emergency procedures — motor failure and partial loss of thrust
questions.keyword: propeller strike FOD ground personnel safety emergency landing zone
questions.text: During a preflight briefing, the remote pilot designates an emergency landing zone (ELZ) on the opposite side of the road from where all ground crew will be positioned. During the flight, a propeller failure occurs and the aircraft begins descending toward the ELZ. What hazard does the designated ELZ address?

answers.text: The ELZ ensures the sUAS lands on pavement, which reduces fire risk from LiPo battery impact on grass or dry vegetation
The ELZ reduces the risk of personnel injury by providing a cleared, designated area for the aircraft to land away from all crew members in the event of a forced landing
The ELZ is required by FAA regulations for all sUAS operations within 500 feet of any road or vehicle traffic lane
The ELZ satisfies the visual observer requirement by providing a fixed reference point from which all aircraft movements can be observed

explanations.a: Surface type considerations for fire risk may be secondary factors, but the primary purpose of an ELZ is personnel protection by providing a cleared landing area away from crew.
explanations.b: An emergency landing zone is a designated area clear of personnel and equipment where the sUAS can be directed in an emergency; positioning the ELZ away from all ground crew members reduces the risk of propeller strike injuries if the aircraft must make an uncontrolled landing.
explanations.c: There is no FAA regulation specifically mandating an ELZ within 500 feet of roads; ELZ designation is a safety best practice and may be required by some operator safety management systems.
explanations.d: The ELZ serves as an emergency landing target, not as a visual observer station; VLOS is maintained through the visual observer positioned appropriately relative to the flight area.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.7 Situational awareness — night operations specific challenges
questions.keyword: night operations VLOS anti-collision lighting spatial disorientation darkness
questions.text: A remote pilot is conducting an authorized night sUAS inspection of a cell tower. The sUAS has the required anti-collision lighting. After the aircraft climbs above 300 ft AGL, the pilot begins to have difficulty determining the aircraft's altitude and orientation due to the darkness and the tower's lighting conflicting with the aircraft lights. Which specific night operations hazard is the pilot experiencing?

answers.text: Photopic vision failure — the rod cells in the pilot's retinas are overwhelmed by the tower lights, causing total loss of color vision needed to identify navigation lights
Dark adaptation loss — the tower lights have disrupted the pilot's dark adaptation, making the sUAS navigation lights harder to distinguish against the dark background
Radio frequency interference from the cell tower transmitters — the sUAS GPS signals are corrupted, causing the altitude indicator on the GCS to display incorrect values
Spatial disorientation and loss of visual reference — conflicting light sources and darkness make it difficult to determine aircraft altitude and attitude from visual cues alone

explanations.a: Photopic vision uses cone cells for daylight color vision; the described difficulty is not specifically about color vision loss but about overall orientation and altitude perception.
explanations.b: Dark adaptation loss is a real concern after exposure to bright lights, but the primary hazard described — difficulty determining altitude and orientation — is more broadly characterized as spatial disorientation and loss of visual reference in a complex lighting environment.
explanations.c: RF interference from cell towers is a possible GNSS concern, but the described symptoms of difficulty determining altitude and orientation visually are not consistent with a GCS display error; they describe a visual reference failure.
explanations.d: Night operations present the specific hazard of spatial disorientation and loss of visual reference; conflicting light sources from the tower can make it difficult to distinguish the aircraft's lights and determine altitude and orientation, which are foundational VLOS requirements; this is a well-recognized night operations hazard in sUAS operations.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.1 ADM models — 3P model
questions.keyword: 3P model Process step evaluate risk options before acting
questions.text: Applying the 3P ADM model during a flight where deteriorating weather has reduced visibility to near-minimums, a remote pilot has completed the 'Perceive' step by identifying the visibility reduction and potential cloud clearance conflict. What does the 'Process' step require next?

answers.text: Proceed with the mission unchanged because the weather may improve, and waiting could mean missing the window entirely
Evaluate the hazard's risk level, consider available options such as landing immediately, repositioning, or continuing with reduced scope, and assess the consequences of each option
Perform the first corrective action that comes to mind because rapid response is more effective than extended analysis in deteriorating conditions
Perceive additional weather data by checking the nearest ASOS before processing any risk — the Perceive step must be fully complete before Process begins

explanations.a: Proceeding unchanged is an action, not a processing step; the Process step requires evaluation of the perceived hazard and available options before choosing an action.
explanations.b: The 'Process' step in the 3P model requires the pilot to analyze the perceived hazard — assess its risk level, identify available options (land, reposition, reduce scope, continue, or abort), and evaluate the likely consequences of each option; this deliberate analysis precedes the 'Perform' step.
explanations.c: The first corrective action that comes to mind may not be the best option; the Process step specifically prevents impulsive action by requiring structured evaluation before performing.
explanations.d: The 3P model is a continuous cycle; while additional data is always useful, the Process step can begin with available information; waiting indefinitely for perfect data is not the intent of the model.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.4 Emergency procedures — loss of control link
questions.keyword: lost link time of action immediate plan pre-briefed response procedures
questions.text: Under best practices for sUAS operations, why is it important for a remote pilot to establish and brief a lost-link procedure before each flight rather than deciding what to do when the link is actually lost?

answers.text: Pre-briefed lost-link procedures are required by 14 CFR 107.49 as part of the mandatory preflight familiarity check for all commercial sUAS operations
Pre-established lost-link procedures ensure that when the link is lost and decision-making is most difficult, the pilot and crew can execute a known plan rather than improvising under stress
Pre-briefed procedures allow the FAA to review and approve the lost-link response as part of the LAANC authorization process
Lost-link procedures only need to be established for operations in controlled airspace; Class G operations have a default FAA-approved procedure that applies automatically

explanations.a: While 107.49 requires preflight familiarization with pertinent information, it does not specifically mandate a formal documented lost-link procedure for all commercial operations; the reason for pre-briefing is fundamentally about decision quality under stress.
explanations.b: When a control link is lost, the pilot faces sudden stress and reduced decision-making capacity; pre-established and briefed lost-link procedures allow the crew to execute a known, previously analyzed response rather than improvising under cognitive pressure; this is a fundamental principle of emergency procedure preparedness in all aviation sectors.
explanations.c: Lost-link procedures are not reviewed by the FAA through the LAANC authorization process; LAANC grants airspace access, not approval of specific operational emergency procedures.
explanations.d: There is no FAA-approved default lost-link procedure for Class G operations; all sUAS operations benefit from a pre-briefed lost-link response tailored to the specific aircraft, environment, and mission.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.11 Emergency procedures — loss of GPS and GNSS outage
questions.keyword: GNSS outage NOTAM preflight check interference testing area
questions.text: A remote pilot checks NOTAMs before a flight and finds one indicating GPS testing by the military will cause GPS unreliable conditions in the operating area from 1400 to 1700 local time. The planned flight is scheduled from 1430 to 1530. Under ADM principles, what is the appropriate response?

answers.text: Proceed with the GPS-dependent automated survey mission because military GPS testing NOTAMs are precautionary and rarely cause actual signal degradation for civilian receivers
Reschedule the automated GPS-dependent portion of the mission outside the NOTAM window, or prepare to fly in manual or attitude mode if the flight must proceed during the NOTAM period
Contact the military installation conducting the testing and request a temporary halt to GPS testing during the planned flight window
File an exemption request with the FAA through DroneZone to receive GPS priority status during the military testing window

explanations.a: GPS testing NOTAMs indicate actual, documented interference that can render GPS receivers unreliable or non-functional; proceeding with GPS-dependent operations during this window is unsound ADM.
explanations.b: Sound ADM in response to a GPS outage NOTAM requires either rescheduling the GPS-dependent mission to a time outside the NOTAM window, or preparing to fly manually if the mission must proceed; the pilot should also configure RTH altitude correctly in case of GPS failure and increase vigilance for potential link and navigation anomalies.
explanations.c: Remote pilots do not have the authority or mechanism to request halts to military GPS testing; these operations are coordinated at a national level.
explanations.d: There is no FAA DroneZone GPS priority status exemption for civilian sUAS during military GPS testing; the military testing takes precedence and the pilot must plan around it.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.10 Human factors — fatigue and sleep deprivation
questions.keyword: sleep deprivation impairment equivalent alcohol cognitive performance
questions.text: Research in aviation human factors has shown that extended sleep deprivation produces cognitive impairment comparable to alcohol intoxication. A remote pilot who slept only 4 hours the previous night is planning a complex sUAS operation requiring close proximity to infrastructure. Under Part 107 and ADM principles, how should the pilot evaluate this situation?

answers.text: Sleep deprivation below 6 hours is only relevant for operations lasting more than 2 hours; a 90-minute mission is unaffected by the pilot's sleep deficit
The pilot should self-assess whether the fatigue level would interfere with safe operation; if it would, the flight must be postponed per 107.17, regardless of schedule pressure
The Part 107 alcohol provision (8-hour rule) extends by analogy to sleep: the pilot must wait 8 hours after becoming fatigued before operating, starting from the time of the last missed sleep hour
The pilot may proceed if a visual observer is present because the observer's alertness compensates for the pilot's fatigue during the flight

explanations.a: Sleep deprivation effects are not limited to long operations; cognitive impairment from sleep deficit is present from the beginning of any task and worsens with complex, demanding operations regardless of duration.
explanations.b: Under 14 CFR 107.17, the remote pilot must not operate if a physical or mental condition would interfere with safe operation; significant sleep deprivation is a recognized physical/mental condition that impairs judgment, reaction time, and vigilance; the pilot must self-assess and, if impaired, postpone the flight.
explanations.c: The 8-hour alcohol rule does not extend by analogy to sleep debt; they are separate conditions; sleep deprivation is addressed under 107.17's general fitness provision.
explanations.d: A visual observer's alertness does not substitute for an alert, fit remote PIC; the visual observer supports situational awareness but cannot assume PIC decision-making or control functions.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.8 CRM — situational awareness management with automation
questions.keyword: mode confusion automation unexpected behavior monitoring alert
questions.text: A remote pilot sets the sUAS to automated altitude hold mode and steps back to check the ground control station display. When the pilot looks up, the aircraft has drifted 80 meters downwind and is now 15 feet above a parked vehicle. The altitude hold mode was functioning correctly but the pilot had not activated the position hold mode. Which failure does this scenario illustrate?

answers.text: Mode confusion — the pilot believed the aircraft was in position hold mode based on the altitude hold activation, when in fact only altitude was being maintained
Sensory illusion — the pilot's eyes were deceived by the GCS display into believing the aircraft was stationary
Automation failure — the altitude hold mode malfunctioned and allowed the aircraft to drift laterally despite correct mode activation
Complacency — the pilot was too comfortable with the automation and did not check the GCS display for the full 80-meter drift period

explanations.a: Mode confusion occurs when a pilot misunderstands which mode is active and consequently misinterprets the aircraft's expected behavior; the pilot assumed altitude hold included position hold, which is a classic mode confusion error common in both manned and unmanned aviation.
explanations.b: Sensory illusion involves the pilot's senses providing false information; in this case, the pilot simply misunderstood the mode, not a sensory illusion.
explanations.c: The altitude hold mode was functioning correctly — it was maintaining altitude; the lateral drift is expected behavior in altitude-only mode; there was no automation failure.
explanations.d: While complacency may have contributed to the pilot stepping away from active monitoring, the specific failure that caused the unexpected outcome was mode confusion about what altitude hold mode does and does not control.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.12 NASA ASRS voluntary reporting program
questions.keyword: ASRS report within 10 days incident date timeliness requirement
questions.text: A remote pilot inadvertently flies within a TFR on a Monday. The pilot wants to file a NASA ASRS report to document the incident and receive the regulatory protection it may afford. By what day must the report be filed to qualify for the protection under the FAA's safety compliance policy?

answers.text: By midnight the same day (Monday) because ASRS reports must be submitted before the next calendar day begins
Within 72 hours (by Thursday) because the FAA's compliance program requires initial disclosure within 3 calendar days
Within 10 calendar days of the incident (by the following Thursday, counting Monday as day 1)
Within 30 days, which is the standard aviation incident documentation window established by FAA Order 8900.1

explanations.a: There is no same-day filing requirement for ASRS reports; the 10-calendar-day window begins on the date of the incident.
explanations.b: 72 hours is not the ASRS reporting deadline; the correct window is 10 calendar days.
explanations.c: The NASA ASRS report must be filed within 10 calendar days of the incident to receive the enforcement protection recognized by the FAA; the incident occurred on Monday, so the report must be submitted within 10 calendar days.
explanations.d: 30 days is not the ASRS filing deadline; 10 calendar days is the defined window for the protection to apply.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.5 Emergency procedures — fly-away and uncontrolled flight
questions.keyword: electromagnetic interference compass motor propeller magnetic field calibration
questions.text: A remote pilot is operating an sUAS near a reinforced concrete building with heavy steel rebar. During the approach for a close inspection, the aircraft suddenly veers off course. The remote pilot suspects electromagnetic interference affecting the compass. What is the most appropriate immediate response?

answers.text: Continue the approach at reduced speed because compass interference near rebar is normal and the flight controller will compensate with accelerometer data
Activate ATTI mode (attitude mode) immediately to eliminate compass dependence, fly manually away from the structure, and land for inspection before resuming operations
Shut down all motors immediately and allow the aircraft to descend to the ground under gravity near the building where interference is strongest
Command a rapid vertical climb to 400 ft AGL where compass interference from ground structures is negligible and GPS lock will restore normal flight

explanations.a: Continued approach toward a known interference source risks worsening compass error and losing control; the flight controller's accelerometers do not substitute for compass heading reference in GPS-assisted modes.
explanations.b: Switching to attitude mode removes compass-dependent positioning, allowing manual control based on aircraft response rather than GPS/compass navigation; flying away from the interference source restores normal sensor function; inspecting the aircraft after landing confirms no damage and recalibration if needed before resuming.
explanations.c: Cutting motors near a building creates an uncontrolled free fall that could damage the aircraft and potentially injure persons on the ground; this is not an appropriate emergency response.
explanations.d: Rapid vertical climb near a building in compromised compass condition risks collision with the structure; moving away horizontally in attitude mode is safer than climbing near the interference source.
