questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.3 Risk management — identifying and mitigating risk
questions.keyword: safety management system SMS proactive hazard identification culture
questions.text: A commercial sUAS operator wants to move beyond reactive accident response and build a proactive safety culture. The operator adopts a Safety Management System (SMS). What does a proactive SMS approach require of the organization compared to a reactive approach?

answers.text: A proactive SMS requires waiting for accidents to occur and then analyzing root causes to prevent recurrence, which is the core of the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle
A proactive SMS identifies and mitigates hazards before incidents occur, encourages voluntary hazard reporting from all personnel, and continuously monitors operational safety performance
A proactive SMS focuses exclusively on regulatory compliance reviews and does not address operational culture or personnel behavior outside of documented procedures
A proactive SMS requires purchasing the most advanced sUAS technology available because technical superiority is the primary driver of proactive safety outcomes

explanations.a: Waiting for accidents and then analyzing them is the reactive approach; a proactive SMS specifically identifies and addresses hazards before they result in incidents or accidents.
explanations.b: A proactive SMS identifies hazards in advance through operational risk assessments, near-miss reporting, trend analysis, and safety monitoring; it fosters a reporting culture where personnel feel safe disclosing hazards without fear of punishment, enabling the organization to address risks before they cause harm.
explanations.c: Compliance reviews are part of an SMS but are not the totality of a proactive safety approach; organizational culture, personnel behavior, and unreported hazards require proactive tools beyond regulatory checklists.
explanations.d: Advanced technology reduces some risks but cannot replace organizational safety culture, reporting systems, and risk management processes; technology is one component of a comprehensive SMS, not its primary driver.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.10 Human factors — hypoxia and altitude effects
questions.keyword: hypoxia symptoms altitude performance impairment sUAS operator
questions.text: A remote pilot is conducting an sUAS survey at a high-altitude location with a field elevation of 11,500 ft MSL. The pilot begins to experience subtle dizziness, mild euphoria, and a feeling that everything is going well despite noticing several operational problems that should warrant concern. What condition may the pilot be experiencing?

answers.text: Dehydration — the high altitude and dry air are causing the pilot to lose fluid rapidly, producing electrolyte imbalance and the described symptoms
Hypoxia — reduced oxygen partial pressure at 11,500 ft MSL is impairing the pilot's cognitive function, creating a false sense of well-being and reducing hazard recognition
Carbon monoxide poisoning from a nearby generator — CO at altitude is more rapidly absorbed than at sea level, causing the described neurological symptoms
Motion sickness — sustained visual focus on the sUAS at altitude causes vestibular-visual conflict leading to mild euphoria in susceptible individuals

explanations.a: Dehydration at altitude is a real concern and can impair performance, but the specific combination of dizziness, euphoria, and reduced hazard recognition is more characteristic of hypoxia than of simple dehydration.
explanations.b: At 11,500 ft MSL, the partial pressure of oxygen is significantly reduced; hypoxia can cause dizziness, euphoria, impaired judgment, and reduced ability to recognize one's own impairment — the insidious feeling that everything is fine when it is not is a hallmark of hypoxia; the pilot should descend if possible and seek supplemental oxygen.
explanations.c: CO poisoning is possible from nearby fuel-powered equipment, but the described scenario emphasizes altitude as the operational context; hypoxia from altitude is the more directly applicable explanation.
explanations.d: Motion sickness from tracking a remote aircraft typically produces nausea and discomfort, not euphoria; the altitude-related hypoxia explanation matches the described symptoms more accurately.

questions.name: Emergency Procedures and Aeronautical Decision-Making
questions.objective: 8.9 Emergency procedures — battery fire and thermal runaway
questions.keyword: safe battery handling charging monitoring fire prevention practice
questions.text: To prevent LiPo battery thermal runaway during charging, which charging practice is most important for remote pilots to follow?

answers.text: Charge LiPo batteries at a charge rate of 10C or higher to complete charging quickly and reduce the time the battery spends at elevated voltage
Never leave LiPo batteries unattended during charging; charge in a fireproof LiPo bag or fireproof container, using a charger set to the correct cell count and charge rate
Charge all LiPo batteries while installed in the aircraft so the flight controller can monitor individual cell voltages and halt charging if an anomaly is detected
Charge LiPo batteries in a refrigerator set to 5°C to lower the electrochemical reaction rate and prevent overheating during the charge cycle

explanations.a: Charging at 10C is dangerously high; standard safe charge rates for LiPo batteries are typically 1C (one times the capacity in amp-hours) unless specifically rated for higher C charging; high charge rates generate excessive heat and dramatically increase thermal runaway risk.
explanations.b: Safe LiPo charging requires: never leaving batteries unattended during charging, using a quality balance charger set to the correct cell count and charge rate (typically 1C), and placing the battery in a fireproof LiPo bag or metal container to contain any fire should thermal runaway occur; these practices are the foundation of LiPo safety.
explanations.c: Charging while installed in the aircraft is not a recommended practice; it can trap heat, makes the aircraft unavailable, and exposes expensive components to charging hazards; dedicated chargers with proper monitoring are the appropriate solution.
explanations.d: Charging in a refrigerator creates condensation risk on electronic connections and does not safely address thermal runaway; the recommended storage temperature for LiPo is cool and dry (15–25°C), not refrigerator-cold.
